column4: The source section's root ز ك و is pictured as growth: a grain becomes seven ears in this account of spending, so giving returns more than the seed placed in the ground.
The source section links the giver to a fruiting palm; here a garden on high ground receives heavy rain and gives twice its produce, while its owner spends seeking Allah's pleasure.
The section's root ز ك و names giving for purification, and this ayah names zakat given seeking Allah's face as multiplying; the same verse contrasts it with ربا, which does not grow with Allah.
The section explicitly distinguishes the root of ربا from the root of رَبّ; this ayah says Allah effaces ربا and causes charity to grow, setting false increase against blessed growth.
The section's crop image reaches its due at harvest; this ayah commands giving the crop's حق on harvest day, joining field yield to an obligation of giving.

The source section's root ز ك و appears in the command to take charity from people's wealth to purify them and make them grow; here the Prophet is the collector the commentary sets beside the self-initiated giver.
The section identifies the ساعي as one appointed to collect charity; this ayah names العاملين عليها among the recipients, placing administrators within the alms system.
Following 9:103, this ayah says Allah accepts repentance and takes charities; 9:103 contributes the Prophet's taking and purification, while this neighbor identifies the ultimate receiver.
The source section's هدي is an animal brought to the sanctuary; this ayah describes sacrificial camels, their marked status, and feeding from them, giving the offering a concrete ritual scene.
The same offering scene says their meat and blood do not reach Allah but taqwa does, and commands magnifying Him for guidance; it joins the offered animal, piety, and هدى exactly as the section does.
The pilgrimage offering is food from livestock over which God's name is mentioned, with a command to feed the needy; this makes the section's herd and sanctuary gift a public act of provision.
The section defines هدي as livestock conveyed to the sanctuary; this ayah names the marked offerings sent to the Sacred House and describes pilgrims seeking bounty and approval from their Lord.
This pilgrimage ruling calls for whatever offering is readily available when pilgrims are prevented, and requires it to reach its place; it gives the section's هدي a second concrete setting.
The section's sanctuary offering is part of a wider rite: this ayah names the Sacred House, sacred month, and garlanded offerings as supports for people.
The section's هدي is an animal meant to reach the sanctuary; here the offerings are held back from reaching it, making blocked passage the boundary to the completed rite.

The giver in the section parts with wealth freely; this ayah depicts people giving food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving it, showing generosity as a concrete release of what one values.
The section says the giver seeks the Face of his Lord without repaying a human favor; this ayah states that food is given for Allah's face without seeking reward or thanks from people.
The section's giver seeks Allah's face; this ayah explicitly says spending may be done seeking Allah's face and that whatever good is spent is repaid in full, relocating return from people to God.
The section's voluntary giver parts with wealth for Allah; this ayah says righteousness is not reached until one spends from what one loves, making the cost of giving explicit.
This account of righteousness includes giving wealth, despite love for it, to kin, orphans, the needy, and travelers; it supplies recipients for the generous act at the center of the section.
This ayah commands giving relatives, the poor, and travelers their due while seeking Allah's face; it joins a material right to the motive the section assigns its giver.

The section contrasts a gift with repaying a favor; this ayah says a right for the asker and deprived is present in the believers' wealth, making giving a recognized claim rather than a personal debt.
The section's crop has a due on harvest; this ayah describes a known share in believers' wealth, a parallel form of a designated right.
The section says worldly wealth cannot save its owner at his fall; this ayah answers the fear of losing wealth by saying Allah replaces what is spent, from whom provision comes.
The section's seed and tree images make giving productive; this ayah calls spending a good loan to Allah that He multiplies many times over.
Like the section's giver whose outlay grows rather than diminishes, the one who gives Allah a good loan is promised multiplication and noble reward.
The section says wealth will not avail when a person falls; this ayah urges spending from God's provision before death arrives, when the latecomer wishes for more time to give charity.
The section's man gives his wealth for purification; this ayah condemns religious leaders who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way, the contrary use of property.
The hoarded wealth in the preceding warning is heated and used to brand its owners; this gives bodily force to the section's claim that property cannot rescue its possessor.
The section's giver seeks God's face rather than settling a human favor; this ayah says spenders who do not follow their gift with reminders or injury have their reward with their Lord.
This ayah makes a kind word and forgiveness better than charity followed by injury, drawing a boundary around what counts as giving that benefits its recipient.
The section contrasts the giver with the one who withholds; this ayah praises people who give others preference even when they themselves are in need.
The section's donor overcomes withholding; this ayah says those protected from the soul's stinginess are successful, naming the inner boundary that giving crosses.
The source section's root ز ك و is used here for one who purifies himself; the ayah says that purification benefits the person himself, clarifying where its gain returns.
The section connects ز ك و with giving and growth; this ayah announces that the one who purifies himself succeeds, with purification as the visible result.
The source section's root ز ك و evokes growth; this ayah says success belongs to the one who purifies the soul, in direct contrast to the following ayah's corruption of it.
The section's root ز ك و names purification, while this ayah forbids people to claim purity and says Allah knows the God-fearing; it also says He knew them as embryos in their mothers' wombs.
Like the warning in 53:32, this ayah challenges people who claim to be pure and says Allah purifies whom He wills; it sets self-certification against God's judgment.
The section distinguishes personal giving from a collector's assessment; this ayah makes charity before private consultation an act that is better and purer for the giver.
The section's giver does not pay back a favor; this command not to give while seeking a greater return marks the boundary between a gift and a transaction.

The source section explains ر ب ب through gradual upbringing; this prayer uses رَبَّيَانِي for parents who raised the speaker, a remembered human favor unlike the section's donor who owes no repayment.

The section reads 92:7's root ي س ر through a lexicon's image of a flock's abundant yield; this matching promise, We shall ease you toward ease, preserves the Quranic ease sense alongside that concrete gloss.
The section says property will not help its owner at his fall; this ayah says neither wealth nor children benefit on the Day when people are raised.
After denying that wealth and children avail, this ayah names a sound heart as what matters; it clarifies the inward end beside the section's act of giving to purify.
This ayah calls wealth and children adornments of worldly life and lasting righteous deeds better; the section's giving turns wealth into an act with an enduring moral value.

The section links field growth to wealth; this ayah compares worldly life to rain-fed plants that flourish, yellow, and become debris, while people boast in wealth and children, making the crop's growth temporary.
The section compares denial of the good to milk drying unexpectedly; this ayah's denier of the judgment is the person whose conduct toward vulnerable people is then exposed.
The section opposes its giver to withholding; the next description of the denier is one who repels the orphan, a concrete refusal of care.
This ayah condemns failing to urge feeding the poor, a direct social opposite to the section's gift of wealth and the food given in 76:8.
The section pairs a giver with one who withholds; this rebuke says people fail to honor the orphan, then continues with their neglect of feeding the poor.
The section's gift releases provision to others; this ayah names the failure to urge feeding the poor as a sign of moral neglect.
The section's giver parts with wealth; this ayah condemns consuming inheritance greedily, the opposite use of property.
This ayah names intense love of wealth in the same rebuke of neglecting orphans and the poor; it sharpens the section's contrast between giving and withholding.
The section's giving is a chosen costly act; this ayah asks what the steep path is, then answers with freeing a person and feeding the hungry.
Freeing a slave is the first concrete deed in the steep path, showing release of another person as one form of giving beyond the section's wealth.
The steep path continues with feeding in a day of hunger, paralleling the provision released by the section's generous giver.
This ayah specifies an orphan near of kin among those fed on the hard day, sharpening the recipients of the section's generosity.
The next recipient is a poor person in severe need; it gives the feeding image a precise human counterpart to the section's charitable wealth.
This parable begins with garden owners who intend to harvest its fruit, matching the section's crop and harvest image before revealing the consequence of withholding.
While the garden owners sleep, a visitation passes over their garden; the sudden loss reverses the crop's expected growth and harvest.
The orchard is left like a harvested field, contrasting a hoped-for yield with a crop destroyed before its owners share it.
The owners whisper that no poor person should enter the garden, directly reversing the section's giver who lets wealth flow outward.
They go out intent on keeping the harvest to themselves, making withholding the purpose of their crop journey.
When they see the garden destroyed, they recognize they have lost the crop; this makes the section's harvest due a pointed contrast to selfish possession.
The owners admit they have been deprived after denying the poor a share; the ayah joins withheld provision to its loss.
One among them asks whether they had glorified God, locating the failure in their refusal to recognize the source of the garden's provision.
The garden owners acknowledge their wrongdoing; their confession contrasts with the section's giver who acts in piety from the outset.
The garden's destruction is called punishment, and a greater punishment remains; it reinforces the limit of crop and property when used selfishly.
This ayah names livestock as warmth and benefits for people; it gives concrete grounds for the section's claim that desert herds are wealth.
The section quotes the flock's beauty at evening return and morning release; this ayah is that precise herd scene.
This ayah describes livestock carrying loads to distant places people could not reach without hardship, another material use of the herd that the section calls property.
The section contrasts increasing and drying camel milk; this ayah calls livestock a sign, names the drink from their bellies, and notes their other benefits.
This ayah explains milk as a pure drink produced within cattle; it gives the section's changing milk supply its bodily source.
This ayah asks whether people see the livestock God made for them and placed in their possession, directly staging herd as property.
The livestock are made manageable for riding and eating; the ayah adds uses to the herd's beauty and milk in the section.
The livestock bring benefits and drinks; this is another direct account of the herd as provision.
This ayah names eight pairs of livestock and says people are formed in their mothers' wombs; it joins the section's paired sexes, herd, and hidden gestation.
This ayah divides livestock into burden-bearing and smaller kinds and permits eating from God's provision, concretizing the herd's labor and wealth.
The sheep and goats are presented as male-female pairs; this connects the section's agricultural dictionary senses of masculine and feminine to a Quranic distinction within herds.
The same male-female question is applied to camels and cattle, extending the section's sexed herd image to its named desert wealth.
This ayah joins spouses, children, grandchildren, and good provision, echoing the section's links between fertile herds, offspring, and material wealth.
The king's dream places fat cows beside lean cows and green ears beside dry ones; it makes livestock and field produce images of abundance and scarcity together.
Joseph advises sowing for seven years and leaving most grain in its ears; this is a concrete way of preserving crop abundance across lean years.
The following years consume what was stored, except a little; this reverses the section's growing flock and fruiting field into provision running short.
A year of abundant rain and pressing follows the famine, completing the cycle from scarcity back to plentiful yield.
This ayah sends rain-laden clouds toward dead land and brings forth fruit; 7:58 supplies the land's distinct response, while this row contributes the cloud and rain that grow it.
The source section names fertile, plant-ready ground and coarse growth; this ayah contrasts good land whose plants emerge by its Lord's permission with bad land that yields little.
The section distinguishes plant-suitable soil from coarse ground; this ayah contrasts neighboring gardens and crops watered with the same water but producing different fruits.
Rain sent down from the sky grows plants from which people pasture animals; this directly joins the section's cloud-grown field to its herds.
The rain's yield includes olives, date palms, grapes, and other fruits; this supplies the very fruiting trees and crops behind the section's growth image.
This ayah says water from the sky revives the earth after its death, making rain the hinge between cloud and growing land.
The fruits of date palms and grapevines become provision; this extends the section's date-palm yield image to a Quranic account of fruit and drink.
Water is sent down in measure and made to remain in the earth; this gives the section's rain-fed growth an image of measured provision.
From that water come gardens of date palms and grapes with abundant fruit; this is a direct field-and-tree counterpart to the section's growing produce.
A tree growing on Sinai yields oil and food; it makes the section's fruitful tree image concrete in another provision-bearing species.
Rain is poured down from above, the opening action in a sequence that moves from watered ground to grain, fruit, and pasture.
The ground is split open for growth, a direct agricultural counterpart to the section's fertile soil.
Grain is brought forth from the split earth, the crop growth that the section also hears within zakat's root.
Grapes and fodder follow the grain, showing the field feeding people and animals.
Olives and date palms follow, matching the section's dictionary image of the palm's yield.
Dense gardens appear in the sequence, extending the field into cultivated abundance.
Fruit and pasture are provided, linking human harvest and animal feed in one ayah.
The entire preceding yield is provision for people and their livestock, making the crop-and-herd meeting explicit.
Blessed rain produces gardens and harvested grain; the ayah gives a direct cloud-to-field instance of the section's growth image.
Tall date palms with layered clusters grow from the watered land, recalling the section's palm yield and abundance.
The rain and palm growth are provision for people, and the dead land is revived; crop growth becomes a sign of provision and return.
Dead earth is a sign for people, and grain is brought out for them; this directly joins land's revival to food.
Gardens of date palms and grapes are made in the revived land, echoing the section's yielding trees.
The fruits are food for people, while the ayah asks why they do not give thanks; it links yield to its source rather than human ownership.
Noah's call to seek forgiveness is followed by rain from heaven, joining purification to the source of growth.
The rain is promised in abundance, directly matching the section's cloud that grows vegetation.
Wealth, children, gardens, and rivers are promised together; this ayah gathers the section's material and agricultural signs in a single promise.
Pure water is sent from the sky; this gives the section's cloud-grown field a second direct rain scene.
The water revives dead land and is provided for people and livestock, explicitly joining crops to the herd.
God sends winds that stir clouds, spreads them, and brings rain from them; this gives the section's plant-growing cloud its motion.
People despair before the rain comes; the ayah adds the reversal from withheld water to received provision.
The effect of God's mercy is seen in earth revived after death; the rain-grown field becomes a sign of divine giving.
Rain descends after people have despaired, and mercy spreads; this matches the section's cloud as a source of renewed growth.
Water makes the earth swell and produce every kind of beautiful growth; the ayah then compares human formation in the womb, joining soil and gestation.
A good word is likened to a good tree with firm roots and branches reaching high; this extends the section's giver-as-fruiting-tree image.
The tree gives its fruit at every season by its Lord's permission, a close parallel to the section's person who grows by giving.
The bad word is likened to a bad tree pulled from the ground without stability, the reversal of the fruiting, rooted tree image.
This ayah names pairs among what the earth grows and in people; it relates the section's masculine and feminine plant vocabulary to paired creation.
The section's plant lexicon uses masculine and feminine categories; this ayah says created things come in pairs, a broader Quranic counterpart to differentiated growth.
The source section's roots ذ ك ر and ء ن ث are used in its agricultural glosses; this ayah uses الذكر والأنثى for the two sexes created from a drop, a human reproductive sense of the same pair.
This ayah says God grants daughters or sons as He wills; it connects the section's fertility and offspring image to human generative provision.
The same passage allows both sexes or barrenness, setting reproductive abundance beside its withholding as the section sets growing and drying milk.
This ayah says God brings out paired kinds of plants; it connects the section's gendered plant vocabulary to Quranic language of differentiated vegetation.
Water produces plants of varied colors, then they turn yellow and become debris; this gives the crop-growth image a clear limit in passing away.
Rain-fed plants flourish and then are cut down as if they had never grown; the ayah contrasts expected harvest with the sudden limit of possession.
Worldly life is likened to rain-fed vegetation that becomes dry fragments; this gives the section's growth-and-wealth image a specific account of transience.
Water is sent down in measure and dead land is revived; this repeats the section's connection between measured provision and crop growth.
Lifeless earth comes alive after rain; the ayah makes the field's revival a sign of the One who gives it life.
God revives the earth after its death; this broadens the section's field-growth image into a direct statement about the giver of life.
The section ties giving to the growth of crops; this ayah commands spending from good things earned and from what the earth produces, while forbidding selection of inferior produce for charity.
After the command to spend from good produce, this ayah sets Satan's threat of poverty against Allah's promise of bounty, a specific reversal of the fear that giving diminishes provision.
This ayah says public charity is good but secret charity given to the poor is better and expiates sins; it adds a private form of the face-seeking gift in the section.
This ayah describes people spending wealth by night and day, privately and publicly, and promises reward without fear; it repeats the section's picture of giving wealth for God.
Those who withhold what Allah gave them from His bounty are warned that the withheld wealth will become a collar; this is a concrete reversal of the section's wealth given for purification.
This ayah condemns misers who urge others to be miserly and hide Allah's bounty, a social version of the section's withholding contrasted with the giver.
Water brings forth vegetation, grain, clustered dates, and gardens of olives and pomegranates; this is a direct rain-to-harvest scene matching the section's cloud-grown plants and yielding palm.

This ayah describes people assigning shares of crops and livestock to Allah and their partners, then misallocating the shares; it provides a concrete contrast to the section's due crop and sanctuary offering.
This ayah says belief and taqwa would open blessings from heaven and earth, but denial brings seizure; it joins the section's fearful giver and denier to the reversal of provision.
Noah calls his people to seek forgiveness, then promises rain from heaven and increased strength; it directly joins repentance to renewed provision and growth.

This ayah says those favored with more provision do not return it to those under their authority so they become equal; its own contribution is withheld surplus, while 16:72 continues with spouses, offspring, good provision, and denial of favor.
A town once secure and supplied from every direction denies Allah's favors and is made to taste hunger and fear; it reverses the section's fruitful herd and crop into scarcity after denial.
The command to give relatives, the poor, and the traveler their due uses the source section's root ء ت ي in a direct distribution of wealth, then forbids waste.
This ayah says that if people owned the treasuries of their Lord's mercy they would still withhold for fear of spending; it sharpens the section's contrast between generosity and miserliness.
Each community is given a rite in which God's name is mentioned over livestock He provided; it joins the section's sanctuary animal to provision from God.
Asked who sends water from heaven and revives the earth after its death, people answer Allah; it makes the source of the section's field-growth explicit.
Water is driven to barren land and crops grow for people and livestock to eat; this is a precise meeting of the section's rain-grown field and herds.
Those who recite, pray, and spend from God's provision are described as hoping for a trade that will never perish; this turns the section's gift into lasting return.
The next ayah promises full payment and an increase from God's bounty; 35:29 contributes the non-perishing trade, while this row contributes its promised return.
When told to spend from what Allah provided, the deniers ask whether they should feed those whom Allah could feed; this is a direct refusal of the section's voluntary giving.
This ayah places night and day, rain from heaven, and the revival of earth together; it connects the surah's night-day frame to the section's rain-grown field.
People are called to spend in God's way and some withhold; the ayah says the miser withholds from himself and contrasts human need with Allah's richness, matching the section's giver and miser.
The section uses the root س ع ي for the collector's work and for varied effort; this ayah says a person has only what he strives for, locating responsibility in each person's own action.
The earth is laid out for creatures, beginning a passage that names fruit, date palms, grain, and fragrant plants; it gives the section's cultivated field a wider scene.
Fruit and date palms with their sheaths are named as earth's yield, directly matching the section's palm and crop growth.
Grain with husks and fragrant plants complete the yield; the ayah makes the earth's provision concrete in crops.
The ayah asks what people sow, introducing a direct crop image behind the section's growth language.
It asks whether people make the crop grow or God does; this makes explicit that the section's growth of field, palm, and giver comes from divine nurture.
God could make the crop dry debris after it grows; this gives the field's increase a specific limit and reversal.

This ayah directs distributed wealth to the Messenger, relatives, orphans, needy, and traveler so it will not circulate only among the rich; it extends the section's alms collection into social distribution.
This ayah warns believers not to let wealth and children divert them from remembering Allah; it identifies one way property defeats its owner, while 63:10 adds the urgency to spend before death.
The command to remind whoever benefits from reminder matches the surah's warning that precedes the giver's purification and the contrast with the denier.
This ayah says the one who fears will take the reminder, matching the section's giver among the God-fearing and the surah's promised ease.
The next ayah says the most wretched will avoid the reminder, completing 87:10's division between the one who fears and the one who turns away as in the section's two paths.
The section's surah ends by saying the giver will be satisfied; this ayah addresses the tranquil soul returning to its Lord, carrying the same stance into the closing scene.
The soul is described as satisfied and pleasing to God, a close counterpart to the section's promise that the giver will be content.
The satisfied soul is invited among God's servants; 89:28 contributes its approval, and this row contributes belonging to the company of the accepted.
The next invitation is to enter God's garden, completing 89:27-29's return and approval with the promised destination.
The ayah says the human being transgresses, setting up the section's description of one who becomes self-sufficient and withholds.
The specific cause is that a person sees himself as self-sufficient; this directly parallels the source surah's root غ ن ي in its description of the miser's imagined independence.
The ayah says the return is to the Lord, a boundary on imagined self-sufficiency that completes the section's contrast between worldly wealth and the giver seeking his Lord's face.
